paper.title_en: Observational constraints on early time non-phantom behaviour of dynamical dark energy
paper.abstract_en: We investigate dynamical dark energy models in which the scalar field component is non-phantom at early times. The models include a single-exponential thawing field, a double-exponential scaling--thawing field, and extensions in which a steep exponential scaling field is combined with a cosmological constant, a constant-$w$ fluid, or a CPL fluid. We confront them with Planck PR4 CMB temperature, polarisation and lensing data, DESI DR2 BAO measurements and the Pantheon$+$ supernova sample. The background parameters are stable across all models, with $H_0 \simeq 67.7$--$68.3\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, so none of the models relieves the Hubble tension. The CPL parametrization prefers $w_0>-1$ and $w_a<0$ at $\sim\!2.7σ$ relative to $Λ$CDM, corresponding to phantom behaviour at low redshift. The constant-$w$ and thawing models remain consistent with a cosmological constant. When an early scaling phase is added, the data limit the peak early dark energy fraction to $f_{\mathrm{EDE}}<0.0075$ ($f_{\mathrm{EDE}}<0.015$ for SC$+$CPL). This requires a steep potential, $λ_2 \gtrsim 30$, and keeps the scalar-field density below the half-percent level at matter--radiation equality. Early scaling dynamics therefore cannot alter the sound horizon enough to address the Hubble tension. The scaling models fit the data as well as $Λ$CDM ($Δχ^2_{\mathrm{min}}\lesssim 1.4$), but they are disfavoured by AIC and BIC because of their additional, weakly constrained parameters. Adding a scaling field to CPL does not improve the fit. Late-time evolving dark energy is mildly preferred by the data, while a simple early scaling phase offers no benefit.
